new.name: trigger_recency
new.mechanism: Intent decays with time between u's own visits, not with list position. For each of u's last 15 items in the last 90 steps, take up to 20 of that item's most recent other adopters and check whether they took candidate j. The co-adoption is undirected on purpose: the time signal comes from u's side, from when u touched the trigger. Three columns: (1) trig_lag, the steps between u's latest visit and the latest visit of u that holds a trigger of j. It is measured from u's own last step, not from A, so it is not a copy of user_recency. (2) trig_tdecay, the capped co-adoption share weighted by 1/ln(2 + lag). This weight decays slowly and does not depend much on the unknown step unit, unlike exp(-age/7). (3) trig_visits, the number of distinct visits of u that contain a trigger of j, which marks an interest u keeps returning to. cooc_last5 and cooc_wsum weight by list position, so a 20-item haul from yesterday counts the same as 20 single visits spread over months.
new.stratum: Users whose recent history spans several visits, so trigger lags differ. They have at least 2 distinct active steps in [A-90, A) and an event in the last 14 steps. new.name: visit_day_context
new.mechanism: What was being bought on the exact steps when u last shopped (u's last 3 active steps) reflects the promotions and drops u was exposed to. The single column is the lift of j's share among the active users of those steps over j's share of the 30-step audience. It separates items that were hot at u's moment from items that are hot in general. The share column is dropped because it duplicates users_30. Visit days before j's first event are excluded, and the lift is set to 0 when j launched after all three days. This way the column no longer encodes 'launched after u's visit', which item_age and user_recency already give.

new.name: recency_state_pop
new.mechanism: Users returning after a long pause buy differently from the average session: they favour basics and seasonal bestsellers over complements of their last basket. Every session in the last 90 steps is bucketed by its completed gap since the user's previous active step (log2 buckets up to 8). Returns after more than 425 steps form bucket 9. Brand-new users' first sessions form bucket -1 and are excluded, which fixes the newcomer contamination. The censoring is now respected: a user with elapsed pause p will return with a gap of at least p, so u is matched to all sessions whose gap bucket is at least u's elapsed-pause bucket, not only the equal one. The single column is j's share in that pool against j's share over all sessions, shrunk toward 1 with a prior of 20 sessions so that sparse long-gap pools do not produce noise. state_pop is dropped because it duplicates users_90.

new.name: basket_size_match
new.mechanism: Items differ in how they are bought: as add-ons inside larger-than-usual visits or as targeted picks. The adopter-activity confound is removed by measuring visit size within adopter. j_addon is the mean, over j's adoptions in [A-180, A) by adopters with at least 2 visits there, of ln(size of the adoption visit) minus that adopter's own mean ln visit size. Heavy users no longer push the value up, because each is compared with themself. style_match is j_addon times u's mean ln visit size in the last 180 steps minus the population mean (falling back to u's whole history when u has no visit in 180 steps). It is positive when haul shoppers meet add-on items or targeted shoppers meet destination items. Both windows now cover 180 steps, and items without data get the neutral value 0 instead of NULL.

new.name: exposure_at_last_visit
new.mechanism: A lapsed user last saw the store at their own last active step tl, so the assortment they remember is the one trending around tl, not the one trending at A. users_7 and users_30 measure demand at A, which is the wrong window for lapsed users. The family counts the distinct users of j in [tl-7, tl] (pop_at_last_visit). It also gives the exposure shift ln(1+pop at tl) - ln(1+users_7 at A). That difference is positive for items that were hot when the user left and have cooled since: they are remembered, and often bought on return. It is negative for items that took off after the user left, which are new to them. For active users the shift is about 0 by construction. Trees cannot form this difference, because the pop at tl exists nowhere else in the model. The earlier launch_vs_last_visit column is dropped: it equalled user_recency - item_age exactly.

new.mechanism: Items follow a typical life-cycle curve: launch ramp, plateau, decay. Regression to the mean of the audience level is already in users_30 and the momentum features. new.name: pair_order_profile
new.mechanism: Direction and simultaneity of the edge i-j among co-users in the last 120 steps, pooled over u's last 10 items i. A co-user pair counts only when both items already existed before both adoptions: j's first event precedes the co-user's step on i, and i's first event precedes the co-user's step on j. That removes the release-order artefact, so a young j can no longer score high just because it launched after i. after_share is the smoothed share of the remaining ordered co-user pairs in which j came strictly after i, among pairs on different steps. It is the behavioural direction among users who could have taken either item first. same_step_share is the share of co-users who took i and j in the same step: items bought in one basket with i, which u skipped in that basket, are less likely to be taken later. Cosine, lift and P(j|i) ignore order. The transition counts measure forward mass only, not the forward/backward ratio among items that were both available.

rival.explanation: The lift may be only very-short-horizon momentum (1-3 steps against 30) or a weekday rhythm, and not u's personal exposure. The twin moves each visit day by 1-7 steps in either direction, keeping it inside [.., A). rival.stratum: users with user_recency <= 3, where visit days coincide with the latest steps

cards.name: recency_state_pop
cards.mechanism: Users returning after a long pause buy differently from the average session: they favour basics and seasonal bestsellers over complements of their last basket. Every session in the last 90 steps is bucketed by its completed gap since the user's previous active step (log2 buckets up to 8). Returns after more than 425 steps form bucket 9. Brand-new users' first sessions form bucket -1 and are excluded, which fixes the newcomer contamination. The censoring is now respected: a user with elapsed pause p will return with a gap of at least p, so u is matched to all sessions whose gap bucket is at least u's elapsed-pause bucket, not only the equal one. The single column is j's share in that pool against j's share over all sessions, shrunk toward 1 with a prior of 20 sessions so that sparse long-gap pools do not produce noise. state_pop is dropped because it duplicates users_90.
cards.stratum: Dormant users, whose pool of returning sessions differs most from the overall session mix: user_recency >= 16. SQL: {A} - (SELECT max(e.t) FROM ev e WHERE e.user_id = cand.user_id) >= 16
cards.null_stratum: Users active within the last 3 steps. Their pool is almost all sessions, so the lift is about 0 by construction. SQL: {A} - (SELECT max(e.t) FROM ev e WHERE e.user_id = cand.user_id) <= 3

rival.explanation: The lift of long-gap returner sessions may just mark evergreen, steadily bought items, because returners after a pause meet the long-lived assortment. That is an item property any user would show, not a match to u's pause state. The twin with hashed buckets keeps the same item-level lifts, so under the rival it helps equally.
rival.stratum: old items (item_age > 180) for all users, regardless of user_recency

cards.name: basket_size_match
cards.mechanism: Items differ in how they are bought: as add-ons inside larger-than-usual visits or as targeted picks. The adopter-activity confound is removed by measuring visit size within adopter. j_addon is the mean, over j's adoptions in [A-180, A) by adopters with at least 2 visits there, of ln(size of the adoption visit) minus that adopter's own mean ln visit size. Heavy users no longer push the value up, because each is compared with themself. style_match is j_addon times u's mean ln visit size in the last 180 steps minus the population mean (falling back to u's whole history when u has no visit in 180 steps). It is positive when haul shoppers meet add-on items or targeted shoppers meet destination items. Both windows now cover 180 steps, and items without data get the neutral value 0 instead of NULL.
cards.stratum: Users with a clear visit style and at least 3 active steps: mean items per active step >= 3 or exactly 1. SQL: (SELECT count(DISTINCT e.t) FROM ev e WHERE e.user_id = cand.user_id) >= 3 AND ((SELECT count(*) * 1.0 / count(DISTINCT e.t) FROM ev e WHERE e.user_id = cand.user_id) >= 3 OR (SELECT count(*) * 1.0 / count(DISTINCT e.t) FROM ev e WHERE e.user_id = cand.user_id) = 1)

rival.stratum: all users equally, concentrated on items with users_30 / users_90 above the median (promoted items)

cards.name: exposure_at_last_visit
cards.mechanism: A lapsed user last saw the store at their own last active step tl, so the assortment they remember is the one trending around tl, not the one trending at A. users_7 and users_30 measure demand at A, which is the wrong window for lapsed users. The family counts the distinct users of j in [tl-7, tl] (pop_at_last_visit). It also gives the exposure shift ln(1+pop at tl) - ln(1+users_7 at A). That difference is positive for items that were hot when the user left and have cooled since: they are remembered, and often bought on return. It is negative for items that took off after the user left, which are new to them. For active users the shift is about 0 by construction. Trees cannot form this difference, because the pop at tl exists nowhere else in the model. The earlier launch_vs_last_visit column is dropped: it equalled user_recency - item_age exactly.
cards.stratum: Lapsed users, last event at least 14 steps before A: user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM ev GROUP BY user_id HAVING max(t) < {A} - 14)
cards.null_stratum: Users active in the last 2 steps, where the window around tl coincides with the users_7 window and the shift is about 0: user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM ev GROUP BY user_id HAVING max(t) >= {A} - 2)

cards.name: launch_cohort_proximity
cards.mechanism: Assortments arrive in drops: items first seen at the same step belong to one collection or campaign and are shopped together while the drop is live. The family gives a kernel sum exp(-|ft_j - ft_i|/3) over the launch steps of the user's last 20 items. Censored items, whose first event lies within 7 steps of the data start, are excluded on both sides. A censored candidate gets NULL, not 0, so 'unknown launch' is no longer confused with 'far from the drop'. The redundant min-gap column is dropped. The claim is exact drop alignment within a few steps, not a general preference for fresh items. The twin therefore keeps each candidate's log2 age bucket and popularity bucket and swaps only its exact launch step, so a freshness preference survives in the twin and drop alignment does not.

cards.name: lifecycle_stage_growth
cards.mechanism: Items follow a typical life-cycle curve: launch ramp, plateau, decay. Regression to the mean of the audience level is already in users_30 and the momentum features. The family therefore isolates the part of expected growth that is due to life stage alone. It backtests on states at A-30: age bucket ab = log2 age, level bucket pb = log2 users in [A-60, A-30), and direction tb = sign of the change versus [A-90, A-60). The target is the realised log growth into [A-30, A). For each (ab, pb, tb) cell it outputs the deviation of the cell's mean growth from the mean of its level-direction cell (pb, tb), shrunk toward 0 by a pseudo-count of 20. The result is then looked up at j's current cell at A. The value is 0 where age carries no information beyond level and direction. It is positive for life stages that typically keep ramping and negative for stages that typically turn down.

cards.null_stratum: Old items, more than 365 steps since launch, on a flat part of the curve: item_id IN (SELECT item_id FROM ev GROUP BY item_id HAVING min(t) < {A} - 365)

rival.explanation: Age buckets may stand in for censoring by the data start, or for a single launch wave, rather than for a generic life-cycle curve. The deviation would then mark one old cohort and not life stage. The twin permutes age buckets among items of the same level and direction cell, so it keeps the cell distribution of ages and destroys only the item's own stage.
rival.stratum: Items whose first event lies within 7 steps of the data start: item_id IN (SELECT item_id FROM ev GROUP BY item_id HAVING min(t) <= (SELECT min(t) FROM ev) + 7)

cards.name: lastyear_phase_transition
cards.mechanism: Seasonal demand is sequential: what people buy after item i in one phase of the cycle differs from what they buy after it in another. Seeds are u's last 10 items i. The seed adopters are the users who took a seed in [A-395, A-365), one cycle before the current phase; their pooled rate is the share of them who took j in [A-365, A-335), the cycle-earlier copy of the horizon. The family outputs the log lift of that pooled rate over j's base rate among all users active in [A-395, A-365), smoothed toward the base. Dividing by the base removes the item-level last-year level, which accounted for most of the old score (R2 0.605 to ag_ly_share_gap). What remains is the user-conditioned, phase-aligned transition. Users without last-year seed adopters get no row (NaN). This includes every user at anchors within 395 steps of the data start, so 'no data' is never encoded as 'no transition'. The cycle length of 365 steps is an assumption, because the time unit is unknown; the half-cycle twin tests it directly.
cards.stratum: Users whose recent items existed a cycle ago, so seeds have last-year adopters: user_id IN (SELECT e.user_id FROM ev e JOIN (SELECT item_id FROM ev GROUP BY item_id HAVING min(t) < {A} - 395) o ON e.item_id = o.item_id WHERE e.t >= {A} - 60)
cards.null_stratum: Users whose items of the last 180 steps were all launched within the last 365 steps, so the value is NaN: user_id NOT IN (SELECT e.user_id FROM ev e JOIN (SELECT item_id FROM ev GROUP BY item_id HAVING min(t) < {A} - 365) o ON e.item_id = o.item_id WHERE e.t >= {A} - 180)

rival.explanation: The lift may be a phase-agnostic long-lag co-purchase transition that would help equally at any lag. The half-cycle twin (lag 182) should then perform as well as the original. A second possibility is that the lift only repeats current cooc affinity.
rival.stratum: Cooc candidates with a strong current co-occurrence signal, where a phase-agnostic transition should already be covered: (user_id, item_id) IN (SELECT c.user_id, c.item_id FROM cand c JOIN ev a ON c.user_id = a.user_id JOIN ev d ON d.item_id = c.item_id JOIN ev b ON b.user_id = d.user_id AND b.item_id = a.item_id WHERE a.t >= {A} - 30 AND b.t >= {A} - 180 AND d.t >= {A} - 180)

cards.name: pair_order_profile
cards.mechanism: Direction and simultaneity of the edge i-j among co-users in the last 120 steps, pooled over u's last 10 items i. A co-user pair counts only when both items already existed before both adoptions: j's first event precedes the co-user's step on i, and i's first event precedes the co-user's step on j. That removes the release-order artefact, so a young j can no longer score high just because it launched after i. after_share is the smoothed share of the remaining ordered co-user pairs in which j came strictly after i, among pairs on different steps. It is the behavioural direction among users who could have taken either item first. same_step_share is the share of co-users who took i and j in the same step: items bought in one basket with i, which u skipped in that basket, are less likely to be taken later. Cosine, lift and P(j|i) ignore order. The transition counts measure forward mass only, not the forward/backward ratio among items that were both available.
cards.stratum: Pairs with availability-controlled order evidence: a co-user of j and of one of u's items in the last 120 steps, with both items existing before both adoptions: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ev a JOIN ev b ON b.user_id = a.user_id JOIN ev h ON h.item_id = a.item_id AND h.user_id = u.user_id WHERE b.item_id = j.item_id AND a.t >= {A} - 120 AND b.t >= {A} - 120 AND a.t > (SELECT MIN(t) FROM ev z WHERE z.item_id = j.item_id) AND b.t > (SELECT MIN(t) FROM ev z WHERE z.item_id = a.item_id))
cards.null_stratum: Pairs without such co-users, where both columns sit at their priors (0.5 and 0): the negation of the stratum predicate

rival.explanation: Even when both items were available, after_share can be high for j in its rising lifecycle phase: its audience is still growing, so co-users take it late. The column would then re-encode item momentum (ag_mom_30_60, trend) and not a behavioural i-then-j order.
rival.stratum: Rising candidates whose 30-step audience exceeds the previous 30 steps: (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ev WHERE ev.item_id = j.item_id AND t >= {A} - 30) > (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ev WHERE ev.item_id = j.item_id AND t >= {A} - 60 AND t < {A} - 30)

cards.name: basket_markov_2step
cards.mechanism: A first-order Markov chain over the consecutive active steps (baskets) of every user in the last 180 steps. P(j|i) is the number of transitions from i in basket s to j in the user's next basket, divided by all transitions out of i. A two-step walk starts at u's last basket inside the window and uses each seed's top-20 successors as intermediate states: score = sum over seeds and k of ws * P(k|seed) * P(j|k). Step units are unknown and visits are irregular, so 'two purchases from now' is counted in baskets, not in steps. The 30-step label window usually spans more than one future basket, and the existing transitions are one-hop. Users whose last basket is older than A-180 now get NULL instead of a walk from a stale basket, so 'no recent basket' differs from 'no path'. The twin shuffles the order of a user's baskets but keeps each basket intact. Co-basket co-occurrence survives in the twin and only the sequential path is destroyed.
cards.stratum: Users active within the last 30 steps, whose next baskets are likely to fall inside the window: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ev WHERE ev.user_id = u.user_id AND t >= {A} - 30)
cards.null_stratum: Users with no event in the last 180 steps, which get NULL: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ev WHERE ev.user_id = u.user_id AND t >= {A} - 180)
cards.sql: WITH e AS (SELECT user_id, item_id, t FROM ev WHERE t >= {A} - 180), nx AS (SELECT user_id, t, LEAD(t) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY t) AS tn FROM (SELECT DISTINCT user_id, t FROM e) d), tr AS (SELECT a.item_id AS i, b.item_id AS j, COUNT(*) AS c FROM e a JOIN nx ON nx.user_id = a.user_id AND nx.t = a.t JOIN e b ON b.user_id = a.user_id AND b.t = nx.tn GROUP BY a.item_id, b.item_id), p AS (SELECT tr.i, tr.j, tr.c / SUM(tr.c) OVER (PARTITION BY tr.i) AS pr FROM tr), lb AS (SELECT h.user_id, h.item_id FROM e h JOIN (SELECT user_id, MAX(t) AS tm FROM e WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users) GROUP BY user_id) m ON m.user_id = h.user_id AND h.t = m.tm), lbw AS (SELECT user_id, item_id, 1.0 / COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id) AS ws FROM lb), k1 AS (SELECT p.i, p.j AS k, p.pr FROM p JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT item_id FROM lb) li ON li.item_id = p.i QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY p.i ORDER BY p.pr DESC, p.j) <= 20), uk AS (SELECT lbw.user_id, k1.k, SUM(lbw.ws * k1.pr) AS w FROM lbw JOIN k1 ON k1.i = lbw.item_id GROUP BY lbw.user_id, k1.k), sc AS (SELECT cand.user_id, cand.item_id, SUM(uk.w * p.pr) AS v FROM cand JOIN uk ON uk.user_id = cand.user_id JOIN p ON p.i = uk.k AND p.j = cand.item_id GROUP BY cand.user_id, cand.item_id) SELECT cand.user_id, cand.item_id, CASE WHEN lu.user_id IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE COALESCE(sc.v, 0) END AS f_x_c3_mc2_basket FROM cand LEFT JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM lb) lu ON lu.user_id = cand.user_id LEFT JOIN sc ON sc.user_id = cand.user_id AND sc.item_id = cand.item_id;

rival.explanation: Two-step mass collects on items with a large in-degree in the transition graph, which are popular follow-up items. The gain could therefore come from popularity among active repeat buyers, not from the chain's personal path.
rival.stratum: Candidates with at least 20 distinct users in the last 30 steps: (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ev WHERE ev.item_id = j.item_id AND t >= {A} - 30) >= 20

cards.name: graph_neighbourhood_momentum
cards.mechanism: Demand travels along the co-adoption graph: when the complements and close substitutes of an item heat up, the item follows. For item j, take its top-20 cosine neighbours on the 60-step graph, built from users with at most 100 items in that window so that heavy users do not dominate. The neighbours' audience is counted without the users who also took j: each neighbour's 7-, 30- and earlier-30-step counts are reduced by its co-users with j. The signal is the heat of other users moving into j's region, not a smoothed copy of j's own counts, which answers the denoising rival. Two columns follow. nbr_trend7 is the sim-weighted 7-to-30 ratio of that external neighbour audience. nbr_mom30 is the log ratio of its 30-step audience to its audience in [A-60, A-30). The id-adjacency trend already in the model uses catalog order, not the behavioural graph.
cards.stratum: Candidates with a small own recent audience, where their own users_7/users_30 ratio is noise: (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ev WHERE ev.item_id = j.item_id AND t >= {A} - 30) BETWEEN 1 AND 5
cards.null_stratum: Candidates without events in the last 60 steps, which have no graph neighbours and get NaN: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ev WHERE ev.item_id = j.item_id AND t >= {A} - 60)

cards.mechanism: A user-user neighbourhood anchored to the user's own clock. u's seeds are the last 20 items of u before A with no age limit. The neighbours are the top 30 users by cosine overlap between these seeds and their items in the last 90 steps: overlap / sqrt(|seeds| * items of v in 90 steps). Users lapsed for more than 90 steps, whose catch-up need is largest, still get neighbours through the recent audience of their older items. The value is the sim-weighted share of these neighbours who took j strictly after u's last interaction, within the 90-step window. A returning user tends to catch up on what their taste community adopted while they were away. A fixed 30-step window, as in ag_ucf30, mixes items that u has already passed over (adopted by neighbours while u was active and ignored) with items that are new to u. Cutting at u's last step separates the two. Users with no neighbour at all now get NULL, so 'no neighbourhood' differs from 'neighbours did not take j'. A 0 now means only an empty window since the last visit or no neighbour adoption. The degree-matched random-neighbour twin is the 'popular since your last visit' control.

cards.name: heat_conduction_niche
cards.mechanism: Heat-conduction (HeatS) diffusion on the 90-step user-item bipartite graph. Resource flows from u's last 20 items to their co-users v with weight 1/k_v, then to j, and is averaged over j's degree with a prior: score = sum_i sum_{v has i and j} (1/k_v) / (n(j) + 5). cards.name: scout_adopters
cards.mechanism:
Cold items have tiny audiences, but who the adopters are carries information. Some users repeatedly take items within 14 steps of launch that later grow; they act as scouts.

The revision fixes three problems:
1. Censoring and era: a user is scored only on items launched in [A-240, A-60), after the data start + 14. Each such item's later success is its user count within a fixed 60-step horizon after launch, so every launch has had the same time to grow.
2. Staleness: old scouting before A-240 is ignored.
3. Popularity: the sum column was a copy of users_90 and was dropped.

A user's score is the mean, over their scored launches, of ln(1 + users in the first 60 steps) when they took the item early, and 0 otherwise. The item value is the mean score of its adopters in the last 60 steps, shrunk towards the global mean with weight 5. Items whose recent adopters are proven scouts should spread next and rank above items with the same small counts.

cards.mechanism:
Users who signed up at the same time (same campaign, season or launch) share entry interests. A user with 1-3 items has almost no cooc signal to show this. The cohort is the users whose first event lies within 3 steps of u's first event.

The revision restricts counts to entry baskets: items a user took within 7 steps of their own first event. The earlier version counted lifetime events, which reproduced users_all (R2 0.993).

The value is the log lift of the cohort's entry-basket share of candidate j over j's global entry-basket penetration. It is shrunk towards 0 with a prior of 20 cohort users, so small and anchor-truncated cohorts stay neutral. The result is a personalised prior for short-history users that compares entry taste with entry taste, not with lifetime popularity.

G4-2 found no first-ever users near the probe anchors, so the target is short-history users of any tenure, not newcomers.

cards.null_stratum: long-tenured heavy users, whose entry basket is old and diluted by later history: user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM ev GROUP BY user_id HAVING min(t) < {A} - 365 AND count(*) >= 30)
cards.sql: WITH uf AS (SELECT user_id, min(t) AS ft FROM ev GROUP BY user_id), eb AS (SELECT e.user_id, e.item_id, uf.ft FROM ev e JOIN uf USING (user_id) WHERE e.t <= uf.ft + 7), fc AS (SELECT ft, count(*) AS n FROM uf GROUP BY ft), fi AS (SELECT ft, item_id, count(*) AS c FROM eb WHERE item_id IN (SELECT item_id FROM cand) GROUP BY ft, item_id), cu AS (SELECT user_id, ft FROM uf WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users)), cn AS (SELECT cu.user_id, sum(fc.n) - 1 AS nn FROM cu JOIN fc ON fc.ft BETWEEN cu.ft - 3 AND cu.ft + 3 GROUP BY cu.user_id), ip AS (SELECT item_id, count(*) AS k FROM eb WHERE item_id IN (SELECT item_id FROM cand) GROUP BY item_id), tot AS (SELECT count(*) AS m FROM uf), cc AS (SELECT c.user_id, c.item_id, sum(fi.c) AS kc FROM cand c JOIN cu ON cu.user_id = c.user_id JOIN fi ON fi.item_id = c.item_id AND fi.ft BETWEEN cu.ft - 3 AND cu.ft + 3 GROUP BY c.user_id, c.item_id) SELECT c.user_id, c.item_id, ln((COALESCE(cc.kc, 0) + 20.0 * (COALESCE(ip.k, 0) + 1.0) / (tot.m + 1.0)) / (cn.nn + 20.0)) - ln((COALESCE(ip.k, 0) + 1.0) / (tot.m + 1.0)) AS f_x_c4_cohort_entry_lift FROM cand c JOIN cn ON cn.user_id = c.user_id CROSS JOIN tot LEFT JOIN ip ON ip.item_id = c.item_id LEFT JOIN cc ON cc.user_id = c.user_id AND cc.item_id = c.item_id

twin.sql: WITH uf0 AS (SELECT user_id, min(t) AS ft FROM ev GROUP BY user_id), ha AS (SELECT user_id, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY hash(user_id), user_id) AS rk FROM uf0), hb AS (SELECT ft, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY ft, user_id) AS rk FROM uf0), sh AS (SELECT ha.user_id, hb.ft FROM ha JOIN hb USING (rk)), eb AS (SELECT e.user_id, e.item_id FROM ev e JOIN uf0 USING (user_id) WHERE e.t <= uf0.ft + 7), fc AS (SELECT ft, count(*) AS n FROM sh GROUP BY ft), fi AS (SELECT sh.ft, eb.item_id, count(*) AS c FROM eb JOIN sh USING (user_id) WHERE eb.item_id IN (SELECT item_id FROM cand) GROUP BY sh.ft, eb.item_id), cu AS (SELECT user_id, ft FROM sh WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM users)), cn AS (SELECT cu.user_id, sum(fc.n) - 1 AS nn FROM cu JOIN fc ON fc.ft BETWEEN cu.ft - 3 AND cu.ft + 3 GROUP BY cu.user_id), ip AS (SELECT item_id, count(*) AS k FROM eb WHERE item_id IN (SELECT item_id FROM cand) GROUP BY item_id), tot AS (SELECT count(*) AS m FROM uf0), cc AS (SELECT c.user_id, c.item_id, sum(fi.c) AS kc FROM cand c JOIN cu ON cu.user_id = c.user_id JOIN fi ON fi.item_id = c.item_id AND fi.ft BETWEEN cu.ft - 3 AND cu.ft + 3 GROUP BY c.user_id, c.item_id) SELECT c.user_id, c.item_id, ln((COALESCE(cc.kc, 0) + 20.0 * (COALESCE(ip.k, 0) + 1.0) / (tot.m + 1.0)) / (cn.nn + 20.0)) - ln((COALESCE(ip.k, 0) + 1.0) / (tot.m + 1.0)) AS f_x_c4_cohort_entry_lift_tw FROM cand c JOIN cn ON cn.user_id = c.user_id CROSS JOIN tot LEFT JOIN ip ON ip.item_id = c.item_id LEFT JOIN cc ON cc.user_id = c.user_id AND cc.item_id = c.item_id

rival.explanation: The cohort's entry basket may simply be the items that were popular at sign-up time, a time-localised popularity. Its gain would then track item age relative to u's first event (ag_age_gap) rather than shared acquisition taste.
rival.stratum: users with user_age <= 60 and candidates with item_age close to user_age

withdrawn.reason: vis_since_launch is a per-user visit count for every item older than 180 steps, so it is degenerate within a user (undefined rho, TWIN-BROKEN). vis_copresent_rate is item demand frequency (R2 0.667 to global_rank). The young-item part overlaps item_age and the per-user clock of G1-7 and of other cards. No fix leaves a distinct pair-level exposure signal.

These are user-level columns that are constant within a user's candidates, so they can only act through interactions. prev_gap duplicates user_visit_rhythm (R2 0.489 to ag_steps_30), and last_sess_n has R2 0.461 to existing columns. The main effect is calibration across users, and the column adds noise for little within-user ranking signal. The pause and visit structure is carried at pair level by the revised G1-1 (trig_lag, trig_visits) and G1-4.

R2 0.835 to ag_pop_decay3, and the random-horizon twin keeps R2 0.689. The column is mostly an existing momentum ratio. Its 1-4 step horizons also invite weekday-phase noise across anchors spaced 30 steps apart.

missed_log is popularity over a window of length user_recency (R2 0.664 to ag_pop_decay3), and missed_share mainly encodes item_age < user_recency (R2 0.696 to pop_share_30). The random-visit twin keeps the same correlations, and the per-user clock overlaps other cards. Trees can build it from user_recency and the existing popularity windows.

dormancy_ratio has R2 0.892 to item_last, and longest_gap has R2 0.699 to global_rank. For sparse items the ratio collapses to ln(1+item_last) and the gap to 0. Revivals within 30 steps are rare positives, so any gain would come from demoting dead fill negatives, which item_last already does.

Both columns and both twins have undefined correlations at both probe anchors, which points to near-zero variance. The idea also repeats segment_pop30 and earlier entry-share cards (R2 0.9 to users_30 and users_90). It is an item-level proxy for an interaction with user_age that the trees would have to rebuild.

traffic_beta has R2 0.886 to trend, and traffic_resid_wk0 has R2 0.928 to ag_mom_30_60, so both re-express existing momentum features. The slope is only identified at anchors where weekly traffic varies, and for young items it fits the launch ramp.
mass_center_frac has R2 0.913 to global_rank, and it repeats ag_peak_ratio and ag_rec_mean_age. Single-event items sit at exactly 1.0, so the column acts mainly as a low-volume and censoring flag.

The neighbour-shuffled twin keeps the card's structure: rho 0.699 against 0.678 and R2 0.632 against 0.625 to users_30. Remapping the hubs to random items of equal popularity leaves the score almost unchanged, so the two-hop mass is recent popularity collected over hubs, which is the card's own rival. It is also the slowest pair query (7.56 s of the 20 s limit) and overlaps ag_ucf30. No revision of the hop set removes the hub-popularity component cheaply enough to justify the cost.

hist_cohesion has R2 0.653 to ag_iuf_cooc, and the neighbour-shuffled twin keeps the same structure (R2 0.666, rho 0.769). The column measures the user's level of cooc mass and staleness, not graph cohesion. chain_support is novel, but its twin is more correlated with existing features than the original (0.423 against 0.107), so the twin cannot test it. 'Stale' and 'scattered' histories are also confounded. The trees can already gate on cooc_hits, cooc_n_last and cooc_mean. Two weak user-level columns would add noise rather than a strong signal.

entry_share is popularity: R2 0.899 to users_90, and the twin check is TWIN-BROKEN (rho 0.928 with its twin). followup_share is weak, with R2 0.172 to ag_adopter_depth and a twin of the same shape (0.291). It is an item average of adopter visit pace, which ag_adopter_depth and the visit-rhythm columns already carry. The sign also fails for short-history users in their entry phase. Neither column is a strong, non-redundant signal.

launch_rate has rho 1.0 and R2 1.0 to users_all, and its twin has rho 1.0, so it carries no launch-speed information. launch_late_share has R2 0.797 to global_rank. Its moving midpoint makes it a 0/1 coin for 1-2 step old items and a stretching lifecycle phase for old items. For young items, trend, users_7/users_14 against users_all and ag_mom_30_60 already describe acceleration more cleanly. A fixed-horizon rewrite would duplicate those columns.

Degenerate. newc_share is constant and newc_lift is an exact transform of users_30 (R2 1.0), because no user has a first-ever event in [A-30, A) at either probe anchor. The newcomer population the mechanism needs does not exist near the anchors. The short-history stratum is therefore old one-off users, which the card does not describe.

silence_ratio has R2 0.892 to item_last and silence_vs_max has R2 0.643 to global_rank. The rhythm normalisation adds little that the trees cannot build from item_last and item_age. The target stratum (items silent for more than 30 steps) sits among fill candidates that rarely reach the top 20. One-step items become NaN and are read as 'within rhythm'. A whole-life mean gap confounds decay with death, and C26 measures the same thing.

The card and twin both time out. Even with O bounded to [A-365, A-180), the target stratum (users dormant for more than 180 steps) rarely has a new item in [A, A+30), so it carries almost no NDCG weight. For active users, old-era links overlap ag_lt_cooc and the seasonality rival overlaps ag_season_yoy. O also grows with the anchor, which adds coverage drift. Cost, drift and redundancy outweigh the small expected gain.

co_support has R2 0.931 to cooc_score and its twin keeps rho 0.895, so it is the cosine signal with a popularity tilt. co_share_j has R2 0.624 to ag_lift_max. The +5 prior on n(j) counted over [A-180, A) shrinks young launches hardest and mixes new items with dying long-tail ones, which works against the cold-denoising claim. cooc_hits, cooc_max and ag_lift_max already let the trees tell one-user links from robust ones.
